source: Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF), General Directorate of Agriculture, Department of Agricultural Extension — 'បច្ចេកទេសដាំដំណាំឪឡឹក' (Watermelon Cultivation Techniques), 2017.
text:
There are two general ways to establish a watermelon crop: sowing seed directly into the field, or raising seedlings first in a nursery and then transplanting them.

When seed is sown directly in the field without proper nursery technique, farmers can face several losses: some seed fails to germinate at all, wasting seed; farmers must spend more time and water repeatedly irrigating the planting holes to get germination; and because germination and early growth are uneven, the crop cannot be harvested uniformly at the expected time.

Seedlings raised directly in the field (without nursery protection) are also more likely to have weak health and be damaged or killed by insect pests and diseases in the early stage after emergence. To achieve high yield, farmers are advised to transplant only healthy, vigorous seedlings.

To raise strong seedlings, the nursery (seedling-raising shelter) should be built in a location with sufficient sunlight and not too close to large trees that would shade it. The shelter roof should be large enough to fully cover the seedling trays, generally built with a roof height of around 2 to 2.5 meters, and covered with a shade net or thin cover that lets in enough light while protecting seedlings from heavy rain and strong sun. A fine-mesh net covering is also used to protect the young seedlings from insect pests. Overly dense or overly compacted seedling media should be avoided, as it can cause seedlings to become weak or drown from excess water retention.
